projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Michael Shuminski was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, Michael Shuminski Jr. Mr. Shuminski served in the U.S. Army with Battery B and the 173rd Coast Artillery. He served in the Pacific Theater, and his highest rank was Tech 5. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Shuminski's home in Monteville, Ohio on October 31st, 2002. Mike was 84 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: I didn't enlist. They drafted me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. When were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: I was--well, to begin with I was deferred twice because they had volunteers. They took them first, the volunteers, yeah. I was drafted in March '41. March 21st, 1941.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you were drafted into the Army?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Army, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what can you tell me about your training, basic training?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: You mean before--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Before Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Before Pearl Harbor, that was Ft. Eustis, Virginia. From--I was inducted. Well, I went to Camp Atterbury for, I don't know, four or five days. Then they shipped me to Ft. Eustis, Virginia, and I was there 'til went to--we didn't know where they was going 'til we was on a train. We were going somewhere we figured, you know, going over seas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Before I forget you said you were deferred twice?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were the deferments for?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Volunteers.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, just because they had--you were draft age, but they had enough volunteers?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: I was draft age, yeah, but they had volunteers so they took the volunteers first, yeah. Yeah, so they deferred me, twice, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So anything interesting or memorable happen during your training?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: No, just regular, regular basic training, everyday routine, out--everyday, you know, going out and drill and your duties. I think it was three months, yeah, and then they--in the time they said, "well, we're gonna go--we're headed somewhere." We didn't know where we were heading, but everybody wanted to go--figured we're going over seas. They figured--well we was, you know, by listen this, and what the commanding officer all them says everything, you know, I suppose he knew about it, but he just didn't want to tell us. That's all, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you go over to Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, I landed Hawaii July 11, 1941. That was in peace time. That was--that was real nice.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What'd you do for fun? What was life like in Hawaii then?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, we done our regular routine. We had off-days, you know, a lot of days I was off, and most the afternoon was off. Whatever we preferred doing - baseball, volleyball, or--no nap. You could nap a little bit but they, "Hey, up. Get going."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you go into Honolulu for fun?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Went to Honolulu, quite a few times; Honolulu, yeah. I've got a few pictures over there. Not too many but a few of them, yeah, yeah. That's quite a city Honolulu, yeah. Yeah, that's a--that's right next to Pearl Harbor, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Not too far, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've been there.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, you've been there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Several years ago.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I never intend--I intend to go, but you know it's a long ways.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I lived in California at the time so it wasn't quite as long.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, okay. It's still--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Easier trip, but it's still a five hour flight, right?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah. Still 23--25--2400 miles, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah, I never--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So where were you stationed then on Oahu?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Schofield Barracks. Schofield Barracks, it's supposed to be--Schofield Barracks, the main post is supposed to be one of the largest ones in the United States.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your job?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Well, my job--we was into radars and search lights. We was in Battery--Battery A in the beginning but afterwards we went to Battery B, 173rd. We was a 98 Coast Artillery at first A, and then afterwards they--I don't know why, but they--after you go down there so many months, you know, days, they shift you around wherever they--wherever you fall in, wherever they need you, you know. So that was in Battery B. My job was--we had a power plant take care of--I was maintaining the unit, the power unit that took care of the power for the search lights, and the search lights were connected with the radars. And radars, it's a--it's a quite a--you probably, maybe you've seen it, I don't know. You know, they got--it's a quite a--it's on wheels. It's on wheels and you gotta go--you may have to move. You may have to get out of there. You may have to--it's hooked with a big truck, big semi-truck. It's mostly stationed on the--on the coast. We're inland but--not the Coast Guard but the other outfit that goes out in the sea--he goes 100 and some miles maybe 200 miles in the sea. It's still on the coast but--what's the name of that outfit? I can't think of it now. But we're mostly inland. Take care of the ones that go close by. Ships or any subs or even planes even--Well, I'm going to far ahead now, I better stay back to Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, exactly. But it was basically the Coast Artillery outfit, right?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Artillery, yeah. It was 98 Coast Artillery.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 98 Coast Artillery.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Afterwards, we was--it was Battery B, 173rd but still Coast Artillery though. But I don't know why they--at that time, I really don't know why they even changed it. Like I said, they wanted it--probably, well they--maybe different outfit, maybe different name or something. So they went from A, B, C, D, you know, that way.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there any tension or sense that war was coming during the fall of 1941?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I can remember. I can remember that. In fact, in fact, I was on guard duty. When you're on guard duty you're on two on, four off. We was--we was, I'd say two, three, four weeks maybe. We knew. We knew. And afterwards, when you're on guard duty--I don't care if you're guarding the barracks or you're guarding the men, day or night--if you were on motor pull, you're guarding the motor pull. If you're in something different, you stay--you're guarding that. No single guard then; there was double guards. Always double guards. We knew. We knew. We knew it was coming.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you're talking about three, four weeks before it happened, you knew.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: I'd say, yeah. I'd say that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have a sense they were going to attack Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Well, not really, but I suppose that's the closest--that's the closest installation to what they ha--Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. But here's how it was. They come down step-by-step before they come to Hawaii, though. That was afterwards. That was afterwards.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. All right let's--

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: I'm getting ahead of schedule a little bit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there any alerts or anything going on the days before December 7th?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: A week maybe two weeks. We was on alert always, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So basically between Thanksgivings and December 7th--

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: They--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --or right around that time?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah. No doubt--no doubt--no doubt, they knew, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what's--

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Because the fleet was always--they claimed--they claimed the fleet was always close to Pearl Harbor. In fact, when they bombed Pearl Harbor, the fleet was only about 3-400 miles maybe closer than that. That's when they--that's when they hit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How about the day before December 7th, on Saturday, December 6th, do you remember what you were doing?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: I was on guard duty. I was pulling--I was just getting off guard duty. In fact, I was in the--I was in the--they called it a train. That's where you wash up and that's where our barracks was. We had to walk, and I had just a pair of shorts and towel wrapped around my neck walking to my barracks. And you heard the planes flying around. They were strafing. All of a sudden they said--"Hell," some of the guys said, "Hell, them maneuvers." All of a sudden they see the arrest signal, you know, they said, "Hell, them is Jap planes," and then that's when it started.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you do?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: What did we all do? We--they all--all the company--all our companies had to get out of the barracks, out of their territory. Our radars were stationed out, our search lights were always in the barracks. We always took them to camp, always to the barracks. Then when we went out, we took them with us. Oh, it just--everybody just vanished away from the--from the area.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Behind the hills or what--

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Well, different places. They stationed--went out in the field, went out close to the woods. I really--I really just can't remember now, but we went out away from the area, yeah. Because at that time, when there was bombing, they bombed most all the--all the installations, all the same time, you know. Bellows Field. Hickam Field. Pearl Harbor. Konowaya Bay (ps). What's the other installation there?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: __....(5 seconds).

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: They hit all the same time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Fort Shafter?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Pardon.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Fort Shafter?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, Fort Shafter. Well, they winter (ps) field too, they hit our barracks, and I think they killed all the males in the barracks. And all the planes were lined up in the airport there--like an air--next to the hangers, and everything. They just went down and strafed them and bombed them. It was a total loss.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember what was going through your mind when you realized you were under attack?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Naw, not really. I've heard guys walk back and forth. They said, "Our lives ain't worth nothin', our lives ain't worth it. Our lives ain't worth nothin'. That's what--what I was thinking, I really don't know, no. I really don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How much of the attack could you see from where you were?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: What they--mostly, mostly it was a suicide. They bombed and strafed and went back to the planes, I guess, to the ship, and another wave come in there and bombed, and what do you call it? That one day, that was most--that was over.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Could you see the harbor from where you were?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Not to--not to--not to visible. Yeah. We was station 'bout, I don't know, 15, 18 miles from Pearl Harbor, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The attack lasted what, a couple of hours almost.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, well it lasted a little bit more than a couple hours, yeah. But seemed to me--seemed to me they--they would have known. We all should have known, I guess. But I don't know why--Sunday morning, mostly everybody's out of camp. The ones on duty, they're on duty. The ones that are not, they're out napping Sunday morning. Yeah so--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what did you do after the attack on that day on December 7th?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: I really--I really don't know. But we just pulled our duty. Stood by and--done what we was supposed to do, that's all. They put us on duty. In other words, I don't care if you were on guard duty, you guard this. You stay here, and you watch this. And what else? What else? I really don't know. That's as far as I know, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were there rumors? Were you afraid they were going to land on the island?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: No, but I suppose they could have. If they had troops, they could have, yeah. No doubt, they could have, yeah. We--everybody said they could have, almost. Because I don't think we was prepared. I don't think we was prepared for that. In other words, it was a suicide. But they had their fleet, like I said, maybe two--maybe closer 3-400 miles, maybe closer than that. No doubt they could have. They could have went to shore, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get a chance to go to the harbor and see the devastation there?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: No. All them places, all the places they're all--they're off limits. Everything off limits. You just--it's off limits like anything else. You're guarded and it's--you ain't--you won't get near there. You won't get near there. I don't care if you want to--you want to sightsee, it's no. That's the thing, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there any moment when you realized what had happened here, did it get to you?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yes, at that time, yeah. It was--it was a scary moment, that's for sure. But I don't know, I think I--I may forgot, but I think we all realized it. It was it, yeah. So--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Backtrack for a second. Did you get along with the Japanese on Hawaii before the attack?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah. We didn't have too much to do with them. We didn't have a--really didn't have to much to do with them, as far as that goes, yeah. Everybody--I mean, the GI's they all--they all called "slant eyes" and "google eyes" and all, but as far as, I think, as far as got along, I think we just didn't get that close, though.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And how about after the attack, what was the attitude toward them?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: I don't know. After the attack, it was the same way. I think it was more scary than anything else. A lot of the GI's said, "Well, slant eyes." They would call them all kinds of names. And one would say "slant eyes" but, I think we both stayed out of our sight. That's--that's how it was, though--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: After the stor--

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: You're a--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: You're, more or less, with the Army. You stay with the Army, you just--you can't get away from them. That's--there's no way. There's no way of getting' away.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've heard stories that there was a fear that there were saboteurs on the island on the Japanese--the Japanese-Americans--

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Well--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The Japanese-Americans were--

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: At that time, I really don't know. I really--I really don't know. That was the--I don't know if we even thought about sabotaging back then, so I really can't say.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you finally come off alert? Was it on December 7th when they finally realized they were coming back?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, there was--was one or two days afterwards, yeah. Yeah, that was one or two days afterwards, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it pretty tense for a while?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: We all was intense then, yeah. Oh, yeah. There was, more or less, like I'd say, suicide. That's it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But your Battery wasn't hit or anything, was it?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: No. We had a--we had one sergeant, he was a communications sergeant. I think he was putting up that night, putting up communication wires and he had wire wrapped around his--he got electrocuted or something or another--it went across the wire, some high-tension wire, somewhere. He got electrocuted, yeah, yeah. Sergeant, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that during the attack?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: That was during--that was that night after.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Night after?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Same night. Same night. They attacked him Sunday morning. It was Sunday night when the sergeant was putting the communication wires up, yeah. He got electrocuted.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I don't suppose you had a chance to listen to FDR's speech on the following day, did you?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Pardon.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you--were you able to listen to FDR's speech on the 8th, on the day after?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: No, not that I know of, no. No, the day afterwards we all was pretty much shook up, yeah. Yeah, we--I don't care how brave--how brave, how young you are, how brave you are, but you know, it gets you too, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what was next then, after Pearl Harbor, what happened with you?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Right after Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Well, we still was--we still was on Oahu. Same place. Did our duties and--and really, really our outfit didn't effected us because we wasn't hit or anything like that. We just done our duties and, more or less, shore patrol and everything and run the radars and the search lights and--and a--but a--after that there was no enemy attack, just at Pearl Harbor. That Pearl Harbor day, December 7th, yeah. More or less--more or less suicide, and that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So did you stay in Hawaii for your whole tour of duty?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah, I stayed in Hawaii 'til 1943, out on Oahu. That same place, yeah, 1943. Then we got--well, we know where we was going because at that time, back at that time no Japs were coming from Japan closer to Hawaii. They were--they was too far from Hawaii. I don't know, do you ever look at a map and check the map everything and study the map and everything? It was right at Midway and that was not very far. Night time we could even see when they have the battle with the ships and everything, the Navy, you could see the flashes. I think Midway was only about 125 miles off the coast of Pearl Harbor, yeah. Another one that was close by was Coral Sea. That was another. They were--they were coming back to--they were coming back to Pearl Harbor. We was fixin', I don't know if we had any--we was fixin' to go back. We had to go back step-by-step toward Japan, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So then where did you go, you said in '43 you left.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: We left '43 Halloween night. In the mean time, we loaded--we loaded--there was always an eight-hour shift, around the clock. Load-up the LSTs. The LSTs, the only one's I can remember, there were only 310 mile--310 feet long. What was I gonna say, miles? And our outfit--our outfit--it's a--they don't call it a battalion. A battalion that a--those are 15 or 16,000 personnel. Our battery put them on four different LSTs. There was no use puttin'--you can't put them all on one, incase it sinks and everything, why the whole outfit goes, you lose the whole outfit. This way you only loose part of them then. You still got the equipment and the men right along wherever your stationed, wherever you're going. So we left--we left Pearl Harbor Halloween night, I can remember. I was standing on that deck of that LST, and that water was just as smooth as this table. That was 1943, Halloween night, and I didn't get off that thing until November 2nd. November 2nd. Of course in the mean time, we left--we was stay--we was at Ellis Island on the way to--we was going to Makin Island. We were going to Makin. There were three different outfits. Another army was going to Apamama. The Marines were going to Turowa. That's where they--that's where they--that island wasn't taken. That island wasn't taken. The Marines hadn't taken it. They said the first and second wave really got battled up. Makin Island we was on, we was--we went there. The infantry had already taken. They had two snipers and most what they called snipers, yeah. They told us not to move or not to--not to be--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: On Oahu? WOMAN: I don't know where-- SWOPE: What's that? WOMAN: I don't know where that was. SWOPE: Oh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were reported dead at one point?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Killed action?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, that was at Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was at Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I forgot about that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, I'm glad you remember. Of course, that's something you wouldn't forget. Yeah, let's here about that.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah, you see at that time, I was drafted from Ashevilla(ph) County. This is Geauga County. We moved over here. We bought this--of course, I don't know if you want that on or not. At that time, there was Ashevilla(ph) County. We was--Pearl Harbor, yes. I was called "missing in action." War department send the word to my folks. Gee, I even forgot about that even. See, how long ago?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: I was in Ashevilla(ph) County, and there was another guy who used to have the same name who was in Ashevilla(ph) City. Ashevilla(ph) City. So, that's where they got--I don't know how long afterwards they got straighten up with my folks, you know, about different names, you know, and different places, you see.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But this other fellow with the same name, he was killed at Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And so they notified your family.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: And notified me by mistake.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But initially they notified your family that you had been killed in action?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Right, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, my.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, yeah. The war department, they sent the word, I don't know how long afterwards, they got straightened up, you know, they--I really don't know. I really--I really can't tell you how long that was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, for a while there your family thought you were gone?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, thought I was a goner.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow. Did they tell you anything about that? I mean, obviously, it's obvious what their reaction would be but did they tell you anything about that, your family?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The families?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: They families, yeah. They said, that I was missing in action, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But then they said, missing in action, and then they notified them that you were killed in action?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: They said I was missing. I was killed in action, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, and you--go ahead.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: See, like we--we was livin' Ashevilla(ph) County.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: And he was livin' Ashevilla(ph) City.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You don't know how long it was before they straightened that out?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: How long, I really don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was their reaction when they got the good news?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: I guess they were--they're really surprised. That's all I can say. They were really surprised, yeah. What they--what they had to say, I really don't know now.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But they weren't angry with the Army for messing that up?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: No. No. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Back then, you didn't get angry.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: I think they were, more or less, glad about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, sure.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow. They didn't have a funeral for you did they?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, Gee. I tell you, they coulda, you know, so soon 'cause after all you're dead, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I mean some times they have a service before they, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: How long afterwards--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They held out hope, right?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: I guess they held out hope, yeah, I guess. We just talked about it not too long ago, you know. There was four brothers. My Dad and mother we--we had a 190--197-acher farm. We had anywhere to 35 to--30 to 3500 cows. When we all went to the service, Mother and Dad stayed up and took care of us and what we had. They was gettin' up at 3:00 o'clock in the morning doing the milking, the chores and everything. You know, back then it was all by hand. There was no milk machine then. It was by hand. They were strong enough to take care of that, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. So you were alive and well and on Makin Island. What else do you remember about that?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah. We landed Makin Island. See, the infantry--infantry--our island, the infantry took that island. When we was gettin' off the LSTs, the infantry was gettin' on and comin' back to Pearl Harbor. They took that island. We was--we was there, in other wards, to fortify it and take care of it. Yeah, the infantry took it. We was there to fortify it, yeah. And soon afterwards, you know, everything, you know, moved in I don't care what it was, you know. Air corp engineers, and the air--regular engineers, they come first though, 2-3 days after they had planes everything in there. That goes 'round the clock. That don't take long when they--when they come in they--they take them trees down put them mats down. Those planes come in there. Ships come in with gas. I walk--I'd be walkin'--I walked through the woods there's nothing to see. Back then, they brought boats with barrels. Gas. They stuck them in the--all over the--in the woods a case--in case a bomb hits it, you know, everything don't go at one time in the air, you know. It was a big set-up. You gotta save--they saved some of this--it was--when the bomb hits, you know, they're--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What chain, do you remember what chain of islands that was a part of, Makin and Turowa and all that.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Gilbert's.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The Gilbert's.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Gilbert Islands, yeah. The marshals were right up close too, right next to it, only 125 mile--there's a--what's that--Itatika(ph), Itaweeka(ph).

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Itawotak(ph)

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Enaewhoa(ph). Yeah, something like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The one left?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: That was the closest one, yeah. And that was pretty well fortified. The Japs had pretty well fortified in there. Yeah, and--okay. The LST I was on, we was in lagoon, we was set there, I don't know how many hours, but we was hung up on a reef. Our L--the LSTs can't go up on the shore, but then I don't know what it is, six foot maybe less to walk, less than that, right to the shore. We was hung up on the--we could--we could see the infantry guys going through and see the tanks. Infantry guys along with the tanks going through. Even before we got off, you know. It was pretty well clear by that time. But there was still snipers in there but we could see the infantry and the tank division goin' with the infantry guys along side of them there. So we was out there. They said the tide comes in every six hours. It goes out and then comes, you know, comes back in again. So we was one of the unfortunate ones to stay in there. But we see the other guys gettin' off in the water walkin' that deep with their everything on their backs, you know. Whenever you gotta to walk to the shore, you got to walk. You can't swim. You gotta to walk so--yeah, that's a--but a--that island was pretty well taken. I mean--I mean, what the--what the Air Corp done, bombed it, and they strafed it with the ships so they--there can't be too much left. The ones that dug in deep, them the ones that--they were snipers, yeah, but--yeah. I was--we was down there nine months, nine and a half months, something like that, and then we come back to Pearl Harbor again. But in the mean time, in the mean time, we were on the coast of Turowa. Get other--the rest of the convoy that come back to the--come back to Pearl Harbor, and that Turowa it was--the island was--there was nothin' but stumps. Like you see the woods, there was nothin' but--you didn't see the tops. All you'd see is them stumps. You know, from--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: From our--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Shelling.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Shelling from the planes and the sea. Oh, yeah, we seen a lot of them. We seen quite a few of them duds. Sixty, eighty duds that didn't go off, you know. There was a few of them down there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Those were our bombs that didn't go off?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah, there--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Defective?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Either defective or it wasn't set, I don't know. I really don't know what that was. But you could pick up a piece of iron. That's a really piece of iron them shells made out of, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you did go ashore at Turowa?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Not Turowa. Makin. Makin.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Makin, you said?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Marines--Marines took Turowa, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you didn't go ashore later or anything, you could just see that from the ship?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Just see from the ship, yeah. We waited for the rest of the convoy, yeah. But--okay. I'm getting a little bit ahead now. Before--before we went to Makin Island, we still was in the Ellis group. I don't know if you look at a map, you know what the Ellis, Ellis Island--what the Ellis Islands are. We was--we was in there three days, four nights, or four days and four nights. I don't know which. Waiting for the rest of the convoy. When we left Pearl Harbor, there was only, I think it was only 16 LSTs, and three or four destroyers. There's always one ahead, the one to the side, the one inside, the one in the back. It'd be always way ahead of LSTs. LSTs was goin', one here. There's about four of them in a row here, I mean, distance apart, you know, same another distance and another distance apart. We all talk--that's all we seen. That's all it was with this. But a day or so before we hit the island, I think it was, maybe it was the same day. Boy, we looked up on the horizon, we could see--we could see ships, carriers--there was four carriers, I think it was, when we went down--battleships, cruisers, destroyers. Oh, my god. We sure was, I'll tell you, yeah. But--you know, I don't know. When you--I don't care if we was goin'. We knew we was goin' to war, but still the guys were laughin' and jokin' and whatever, you know. You're not--you're not gonna go with a gun and say, "Well, we're gonna go get them." Part-time we laughed. Part-time we cried, so. Yeah, but a--we was down there nine months, maybe a little over nine months. I came back to Pearl Harbor and then they get--then a--I guess we was--I was at Pearl Harbor, I don't know, three or four months. I think about three months at the most. And then we had a kind of a rotation, point system. I can remember, I think, I had about the second highest, I think, 117 or 114 points. Ones that had more points, I think 121 or something like that, they went first, goin' to the states. When I left '41, Pearl Harbor overseas, I never seen the states 'til I come back. Yeah, then they got a rotating point system. I didn't want to go by boat. I didn't want to go by plane. But at that time I would have went any way. I didn't care. I said it now, but I don't know what I said at that time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So this would probably be what, late 1944?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah, that's--no, that'd be early--earlier--early '44, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, you said you were nine months on Makin?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: From Halloween basically 'til--

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That would put you into the summer of '44 you were on Makin.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah, summer.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And then three months on Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Two, three months. So, yeah, some time in '44.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah, when I got discharged it was in July '44, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: July '44 is when you got discharged?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you actually get home?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: I don't know. Was that July of '44 or '45?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Maybe July of '45?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: '45, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you home before you were discharged?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were discharged and then sent home?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Then sent home, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So maybe you were in Pearl 'til '45, you think, when you went back?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: '45? Let's see. I'd have to see my discharge paper. I've got my discharge paper.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, you'll need to dig those out 'cause there's some things you'll need to fill out anyway. So if you've got them available, that'll help. That'll be on that form, so that's okay. So you finally got home, whenever that was. When did you see your family? How long did it take you to get home? Long trip?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: No, I don't think it was very long. I gotta think now. Oh, I got the--let's see. Up off of the--no, wait. We was--we come back--we come back from overseas then we was--I did come to the states and that was to Fort Croncrite, California when they had the big tree, when they had the big tree meeting, they sent us back to California in case they had a riot or something, so we stand by there. So I got discharged from California, yeah. Then I went to Indiana camp, I don't know, Camp Atteria (ph). Camp--what's the other camp? I had it earlier. Atterbury. What's the other one? Let's see. I think it was Camp Atterbury, yeah. But, dam it's gone and been a good many years now. I can't remember. December 7th goin' to be--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Coming up on another anniversary.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what was that reunion with your family like after they had thought they had lost you?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: I don't know. It just was a reunion. That's all it was. They were glad to here that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have a party?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: No, not really. I don't think they had a party. I don't remember though.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So were you back home when they dropped the atomic bombs?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, yeah. That was in '45.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. August of '45.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: August, yeah. Yeah, I was home then, yeah. I'm pretty sure, yeah. I got discharged in '44, yeah. Yeah, I was home then, yeah. That's when the--yeah, I was home then, yeah. I was home when they discharged that bomb, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What'd you think when you heard that?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, I don't know. But I thought that was alright. I don't know. That was Jimmy Dolittle.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, Jimmy Dolittle was earlier.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He bombed Tokyo.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: He bombed Tokyo, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: With the atomic bombs with the olagay (ph) and the tibbit's as the pilot of the olagays.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What--do you remember--any memories of VJ Day when the Japanese finally surrendered?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah, we was glad to here that. END OF TRACK ONE; BEGIN TRACK TWO. SWOPE:

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you don't remember having any particular celebrations on VJ Day?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: No. I really don't know. I can't remember that far back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you married when you were in the service?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: No. I was just--I was just a teenager--not a teenager but--yeah, just a youngster.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You met after the war then?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: We got married.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I said, "You met after the war?"

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, yeah. After the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything about getting letters from home while you were overseas?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, yeah. They always said everything was okay. Spring time everything, okay. And then start plantin', and everything's goin'.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they sent you any goodies any packages?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah. Back then we got all kinds of goodies, yeah. But after a while, like during the war, everything was censored, you know, you couldn't--you couldn't ship nothin'. You know, everything was censored, you know, goin' out or comin' in there, so--so that was--well, everybody knew what they had to send, you know. Any kind of photos or pictures or any kind of--well, you had everything was off-limits. You couldn't take cameras. You couldn't take the pictures to begin with so--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things did you write back home?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Well, during the war, you know, they censored--they censored all the mail and everything. Everything's okay. Everything's fine. We're on duty. We're all--this buddy and this buddy and--you know. Had a lot of good buddies though, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What are your memories about your buddies? Tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Well, man, tell you the truth, as far as addresses or anything, all them years, I don't have any of the addresses. In fact, one guy did come over with his wife. I don't remember. I don't remember. After the war, that had to be--that had to be back, maybe '60s. One guy from Indiana, him and his wife come over. In fact, I was workin'. I came home, open the door, they was there--what, who is this? But I recognized him right away. Yeah, he was one of the truck drivers for the mail and brought the rations, you know, the rations, you know, and brought the mail. Had the other buddies but--I don't know, they were all good buddies though. Oh, man.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things did you do together when you were overseas during the war with your buddies?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: You mean what kind of--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Things for entertainment, that sort of thing.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, entertainment. Oh, yeah. Like we was in Pearl Harbor if you went to--if you went to the joint, the drinkin' joint, why if you got in there by 10:00 O'clock, you're lucky. Otherwise, it's filled up, you know. Pearl Harbor is nothing but soldiers and sailors. Honolulu was nothing but sailors and soldiers back then, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did any shows or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, yeah lots of shows, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You enjoy shows?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, yeah lots of shows, yeah. In fact, they had a big theater, show theater right at our post. A lot of pineapple fields. A few banana fields. Coconut fields. Coconut patches.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies during the war?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: No. We lost--my God, we did lose one, goin' down on the LSTs. Forgot about that too. You know when you cross the equator, which we did cross the equator goin' and comin' back, everybody got initiated, whether they gab you and cut your hair and whatever, however you wanted it--not you wanted it, they cut the way they--the way they was goin' to cut it. So we had one not on our LSTs but on some other LST. He fell off from the bows somewhere, and all the ships had a half mass for him and buried him at sea before we went down to the invasion even, went to the island even. I often thought about that, about their parents. How did the Army or the--the--how they notified their parents about what happened to them, you know. Got buried at sea on the way over or killed in action, or missin'. How they ever reported that, I really--I really--I've thought--I've thought of that many times. We always--I've always talked to my wife about--what did they--what information did they give to their parents then. But he was--before we got to the islands, they buried him at sea.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So he fell overboard during the celebration as or whatever they--

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah. He fell off a bow on ship, somethin' or another, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He didn't fall--did he fall overboard?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: No. No. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, he fell on the ship?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: He fell on the ship, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This was during the crossing of the equator--

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Goin', yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --initiation, whatever.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Initiation across the equator, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You're right. How would they notify if they're killed in action?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: That's what I was wondering, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Or died--died in action or whatever, however they--

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: I really don't know how they--how they--how they relayed the message to the parents. I couldn't tell you about that. Often thought of that, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, of all the ways.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah but you know there's--well I don't know. A few times--a few times when I was overseas, I don't care if I was at Pearl Harbor or at Makin Island, I'd look across that water as far as your eyes could see. I'll never see the states again. There's a few times I thought of that, yeah. But that's--you often--you often wonder, I mean being--you know, got shipped overseas. You're a different place already from the United States, you know. Course Hawaii was the territory of the United States, still it's overseas. That's a 100--224 miles or 321--2300 miles, so. Yeah, I--I consider myself fortunate though, where I've been. I I've met a few guys been in the jungles, Pacific, Guadalcanal, or New Guinea, or Iwo Jima; all them places. They--they was some jungle, some fightin'. I noticed they told us a lot of times too, first three or four days on the island, don't even get up to go to the bathroom. Of course, first thing was mosquitoes. The mosquitos were so bad they put a net up to sleep under, to get under. The mosquitos by night, especially at nighttime, you know. If you had to go to the bathroom, you didn't dare to be movin' around because one of your own men, you know, in the dark, you prowl around, one of your own men would shoot you not--not wantin' to shoot you but they--they think a Jap--it's a sniper walkin' around, a Jap walkin' around, you know. So they told us all that story to be cautionate (ps).

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close encounters with snipers or anything?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: No. Well--we had a few snipers there. They caught them. Most of them. They--most of them. They'll live a long time 'cause they got mostly all coconuts on the island. Them trees are all coconuts. Either you drink the juice or eat the coconut itself, you know. You're up in a tree, a coconut tree, it's all pretty well hidden. If you're not in the jungle, you're in a cave somewhere. I don't know, them caves, at that time they were pretty well--some of them places, I know, I heard they had to use them flame-throwers to go back and send them--I guess some of them guys really told you some stories that are worse than I am.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They're all very interesting to me.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: All this.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: A small percentage of guys were under fire. I mean, most of the stories are not of being under fire.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah, well--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think of that experience overseas, does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: We was--we was no where--of course, they say. They tell you, you know, be cautious. You can be doin' somethin' to somethin', you don't know who. It could be a sniper that come up, shoot you, stab you, bang you in the head or whatever. But, nobody knows themselves because if they're hidden--we was in a place not some of the jungles like some of the places, they are, were really bad places. But--I think we was pretty fortunate a few snipers but that wasn't--they could--they could be on the island for two, three months, maybe longer. Some of them there more than that. But if they ain't got no kind of ammunition or any kind of a gun, if they don't capture 'em or somethin', they could live for the longest time. Maybe you could get in touch with them, they could bump you off. Who knows, yeah. But I a--I always thought I was pretty fortunate. A good many--I spent four years and four months and nineteen days in the service. I'll never forget that. That's one thing I'll never forget.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that would put your discharge in 1945 then? July of--four years, four months. And you said you went in March of '41?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: March '41, 23rd, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, you discharged in July of '45.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Okay. That was--that could be the '45 then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That sounds right from what you've told me?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You think that covers it? Anything else?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: I don't know. I probably missed a lot of stuff. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your highest rank?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: My highest rank. I was a Corporal Technician, that's the highest, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's like at T5 or--

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah, that's it. Yeah, I was going to tell you the power plant that I was operating. It's a machine. It's about from here to the wall long, about so high. It's a power unit that throws that light into action and that's supposed to be--that's--they said you could hold a newspaper eight miles and read it. What--what kind of power that is, it's a--when the when the man you're the operator of the power plant--I was the first man that's supposed to be run out there and start that motor up and let it run, and let it get--just like anything else. You used to take your car and start it up, let it warm up then it's gonna--just like anything, it'll run better. When that man throws that light into action, of course the light sets out little ways from the power plant unit, and your radar sets out further yet. And when those candles hit together, I forgot what the--what the--what is the power that, that throws that light into action? Oh, you've probably seen them lit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've seen search lights, yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: They say you could hold a newspaper up to eight miles and read the read the newspaper. With the--when we was on Makin Island, I don't know how many--how many times the Japs come over. You're--you're on alert. You're in the bunks but with your shoes and your clothes and everything. The minute that siren goes, you better get your butt out there and go and do something because a--do your job, or else get out of your bunk because you don't know where that bombs going to hit. If you got trenches, you go to trenches, whatever. My job was get that power plant goin' so the man puts the light in action so he'd have light running when he shines that light up. There was four--I don't know, four or five times when the Japs come over at nighttime. Illuminate that plane with the search light and our 90s that was connected to our outfit. The 90s. That was connected to the search lights. When the radars on target then the gun batteries, they were on target the same way. And those 90s--back then, 90 meters that was the highest. There was--I think there was--I don't know what it was, 90--I forget how many thousand feet, and they shot down a few planes. But most of the time they just sneak attacked. They'd maybe come to the island, or go away. Come to the island, go away. I don't know how many times, four or five times, maybe half dozen, maybe more. You have to get out--when the sirens blows, you gotta get out of your bunk. You don't know what--where that's gonna--a lot of times, I'll tell you what, when the alert comes off, they said the alert was done. And how every now and then a plane comes in without anybody--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Nobody saw it?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Nobody--the radar didn't even--didn't even show on the radar.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Because they would come in so low?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Pardon.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it because they came in low?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: No, they just came over the island. They just came over the island. Dropped the bomb and that's it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was the radar because it's only one plane, do they just not--

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Well the radar shows--the radar can show there can be a squadron of planes or one plane or--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They weren't alarmed when they saw only one blip maybe?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Well, I don't--I really--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But they did get through sometimes?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Every now and then, once in a while, yeah. They got through, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you say the search lights could shine up to eight miles in the air?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: They said--they said eight miles you could read the newspaper.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Even eight miles away?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That should cover most of the altitude of the bombers.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The ones at a thousand feet

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, that lit up the area, yeah. Yeah, my job was to keep that gas tank full. Keep the gas in there and oil. And that plant was supposed to be spotless.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was the generator that powered the search light?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: That's right. Generator that powered the search light, yeah. And that plant was supposed to be spotless. The guy come around with his finger, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get along okay with the officers?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. We had good officers, yeah. Yeah, good captains. Most of our outfit--Captain, and there's First Lieutenant and Second Lieutenant. Oh, yeah. I got--I got no--no bad time while I was in service, no, no. ___+.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Stayed out of trouble?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you must have a good conduct metal?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. You better believe it. Conduct metal and I don't know how many ribbons. Yeah, like I said, I've got three battle stars, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Pearl Harbor, Bacon, and what was the 3rd one? Was it the Ellis Island thing or--

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Oh, the bombing of Ellis Island, yeah. We was in Lagoon, Station Lagoon, overnight waitin' for the rest of the convoy there but still there was--it was--you know, they could have come over the lagoon and bombed--they bombed the--is the--you know, every--American installation, you know. We was there. So, any--any--any--you're--you're--you're in enemy territory. Any kind of a bombing, you're--you're--you're entitled to a battle star, yeah. All the--they're written. They're written out. You don't get them for nothing, you know. It's authorized by the commander and everything. In other words, if you're in enemy territory and you're under fire, that's--that's--that's, yeah. Around Pearl Harbor, you couldn't get nowhere near Pearl Harbor. Because, you know, everything was off-limits, you know. You can't be--you ain't be walkin' around. Somebody ask you, "What are you doing?" You can't tell them you're just nosey. Hey, get your--you don't get your butt out, you just get hauled out. See what this guys doing in here, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were there rumors about how devastating that attack had been though?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yes, I guess, quite a bit of rumors, yeah. They said the general of the island, General Short he was--I don't know if he was doing his duty or he was asleep or whatever. And as far as the--admiral of the fleet.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Kimmel?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Nimitz. Nimitz.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I think it was Kimmel at Pearl, right? Or the admiral?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: No. Just the Nimitz--Nimitz.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was the overall admiral in charge of the fleet, right?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah. Nimitz. Nimitz. Yeah, what was--what was he doing so, who knows. Who knows really, really. Them the first guys that them stepped on, yeah. So my--my opinion, that shouldn't have happened.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: As far as those guys getting the ax?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah. I think--I think both of them got the ax.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, Kimmel and Short.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Short.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Kimmel was in charge of the Navy on Hawaii.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah, Oahu, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And so he--he--both of them were--

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: {Coughs}

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: --for not being ready.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. But still like in peace time, I mean, after all what was--what was that fleet off the coast? That coast, I mean--I mean--they had our planes flying around. They should have spotted them, seen what was going on, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: They say at time we didn't have anything over there at Pearl Harbor. They had to ship everything from the states down there. Planes overhead. I don't know if we had enough back then. That's why that war took so long, yeah. Well anyhow--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, one Pearl Harbor survivor, I don't know if this is shortly after the attack, on the bulletin board--I don't know if this Schofield Barracks or not--on the bulletin board somebody had put up, 'Don't be caught short with your Kimmle.'

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Well--well they made all kind of remarks about that. Oh, I know. You always find one, two, or three in the outfit that are--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Jokers?

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: You better believe it. I don't know how--how the word gets by but how'd they getting away with it, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, exactly.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: That's the truth. That's the truth. A lot of times even our outfit too, you know, a guy--a butch would walk--I mean, drive with horse on the horse back, you know. They'd yell, "high-ho silver," or somethin' like that, you know. Jesus Christ, that person, you get reported, that was the general. And our first sergeant, he just (bore) us to death.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Well, we all said we can't see the bars on the shoulders so--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Honest mistake.

sp.speaker: Michael Shuminski
sp.p: Yeah, honest mistake. That's the truth. END OF TRACK TWO
